hops.afterHeading: Build the rise: gradient, channels and removal
hops.title: The fish that hums at 200 beats a second
hops.text: A male oyster toadfish courts mates with a hum called a boatwhistle, made when the muscles on its swimbladder contract about 200 times a second. Each beat needs a burst of calcium and then a quick drop in free calcium so the muscle can relax, and the toadfish's relaxation has become about fifty times faster. The buffer parvalbumin holds most of the released calcium until dense calcium pumps catch up between calls. Myosin lets go of actin fast, and calcium probably comes off troponin fast too. The price is strength: at swimming rhythms, gram for gram, it makes one-twentieth the power of the fish's slow swimming muscle.

sources.citation: Rome LC, Syme DA, Hollingworth S, Lindstedt SL, Baylor SM (1996) The whistle and the rattle: the design of sound producing muscles. Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A 93(15):8095-8100.
Rome LC (2006) Design and function of superfast muscles: new insights into the physiology of skeletal muscle. Annu Rev Physiol 68:193-221.

hops.afterHeading: Where and how often: the evidence and its limits
hops.title: Watch a calcium wave fold a touch-me-not leaf
hops.text: Find a touch-me-not plant (Mimosa pudica) at a garden shop or greenhouse and gently tap the tip of one leaf. The plant has no nerves or muscles, yet its pairs of tiny leaflets fold shut one after another down the stalk, like dominoes. In 2022, researchers imaged cytosolic calcium in living touch-me-not leaves and watched a calcium wave travel down the stalk at about five to six millimeters per second, folding each pair of leaflets just behind it. When they blocked the folding with lanthanum, a calcium-channel blocker, hungry grasshoppers stayed more than twice as long and ate about twice as much leaf.

sources.citation: Hagihara T, Mano H, Miura T, Hasebe M, Toyota M (2022) Calcium-mediated rapid movements defend against herbivorous insects in Mimosa pudica. Nat Commun 13(1):6412.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A fingertip gently tapping the end of a potted touch-me-not plant frond whose nearest leaflets are folding shut in sequence.
image.caption: After a gentle tap, watch the leaflets fold in order as a calcium signal travels along their stalk.

hops.afterHeading: Seeing calcium without confusing the signal
hops.title: The chemical disguise that slipped calcium chelators into cells without poking them
hops.text: Before 1981, getting a calcium chelator or indicator into a living cell usually meant microinjecting cells one at a time. That made it a tough way to study small cells such as red blood cells or lymphocytes. The chelators Tsien worked with had four negatively charged arms that grab calcium, and those same charges kept them from crossing the oily plasma membrane. Roger Tsien gave them a temporary disguise. He capped those four charged groups, and the molecules slipped across intact membranes. Inside the cell the caps were split off again, regenerating the charged chelator and trapping it there, in red cells, mast cells and lymphocytes alike.

sources.citation: Tsien RY (1981) A non-disruptive technique for loading calcium buffers and indicators into cells. Nature 290(5806):527-528.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: Three small glass flasks glowing softly pale blue-green beside a microscope under a warm desk lamp on a wooden bench.
image.caption: Capping a chelator's charged arms let whole cells take it in and trap it, with no needle at all.

audio.title: A chess-piece microbe, three genes for one protein, and a plant that counts touches
audio.transcript:
Calcium is a single charged atom, yet cells turn its comings and goings into steering, switching and even a short memory. Here are three true stories where one simple ion runs the show.

Start in a drop of pond water with a single-celled Paramecium. It rows forward using thousands of tiny hair-like cilia. Bump its front end into an obstacle, and voltage-gated calcium channels open right in those cilia. Calcium rushes in, the cilia reverse their stroke, and the cell backs up, turns, and swims off another way. In the nineteen seventies, biologist Ching Kung isolated mutants that could not back up. Bump them into a barrier and they just kept pushing straight ahead. They were named Pawn, after the chess piece that can only move forward. For decades nobody knew why their calcium channels failed. Later researchers found that two Pawn genes do not build the channel at all; they make small helper proteins the cell needs to get its calcium channels into the cilia. Open a Pawn cell's membrane and hand calcium directly to the cilia, and they reverse on cue. The steering gear was fine. The local calcium door just never got installed.

Once calcium gets in, a sensor has to read it, and calmodulin is one of the busiest readers in your body. In mammals, including you, calmodulin has to fit more than three hundred different target proteins. Its sequence has barely changed over evolution, and in people, some single changes to it cause life-threatening heart disease. Stranger still, mammals keep three separate genes for it, called calm one, calm two and calm three, and all three build the exact same protein, amino acid for amino acid. That quirk has tripped up real scientists. In twenty twenty-four, Mads Munk and Martin Berchtold at the University of Copenhagen pointed to forty-four published papers that used supposedly gene-specific calmodulin antibodies, or mis-annotated databases, to claim roles for one of the three genes. Because all three genes make the identical protein, no antibody can tell their products apart. Three blueprints, one calcium reader.

Finally, calcium does not only tell cells where to act. It can also keep time. A Venus flytrap sits open with tiny trigger hairs inside its leaf. Brush one hair once, and the trap usually stays open. Brush a hair a second time within about thirty seconds, and it usually snaps shut. How does a plant with no brain remember the first touch? In twenty twenty, Hiraku Suda, Mitsuyasu Hasebe and colleagues engineered Venus flytraps with a glowing calcium sensor and watched the leaf light up. The first touch launched a rise of cytosolic calcium that started in the trigger hair and spread across the leaf blade, and then the calcium level slowly sank back down. When a second touch came soon enough, the new rise built on the leftover calcium and reached a higher level, one that went along with the trap snapping shut. After about thirty seconds, too much had faded for the second rise to get there. Wait too long, the calcium fades, and the plant forgets the first touch ever happened.
